content: Sulfathiazole is an organosulfur compound that was historically used as a short-acting sulfa drug. It is classified as an organic compound. In the past, it was commonly employed both orally and topically as an antimicrobial agent. However, its use has significantly declined due to the development of less toxic alternatives. Despite this, sulfathiazole is still occasionally utilized, sometimes in combination with other compounds such as sulfabenzamide and sulfacetamide. It is also used in aquarium settings. The compound exists in multiple polymorphic forms. In its solid state, the imide tautomer is the predominant form, where the proton is located on the nitrogen atom within the ring structure, rather than the configuration depicted in some chemical representations. Sulfathiazole has been referenced in various cultural works. It is mentioned in chapter 104 of Kurt Vonnegut's novel Cat's Cradle, as well as in his New Dictionary and several of his short stories. The 1946 novel Mister Roberts by Thomas Heggen describes the use of sulfathiazole for the treatment of gonorrhea. Additionally, Sonya Dorman's 1966 short story When I Was Miss Dow includes a reference to the compound. The 1998 film Dead Heat also mentions sulfathiazole as a drug used in the reanimation of deceased bodies. Furthermore, in John Irving's novel The World According to Garp, sulfathiazole is referenced in chapter 1, where the protagonist's mother observes it being dispensed to soldiers during World War II.
